children: U.S. oil executives are struggling to plan investments and production as the Iran war drives sharp swings in crude prices, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas’ latest quarterly energy survey.
For investors, the survey points to an unusual combination of higher oil-price expectations and continued reluctance among producers to aggressively expand output.

Executives now expect U.S. crude prices to average $82 a barrel a year from now, about 5% above their forecast three months earlier. Yet volatility, rising costs and supply constraints could limit how quickly shale producers respond to stronger prices.

West Texas Intermediate crude has risen about 36% since the Iran conflict began in late February. Several executives surveyed by the Dallas Fed said uncertainty surrounding the war and U.S. policy has made forecasting increasingly difficult, while generally pushing expectations for oil prices higher.

The Dallas Fed collected responses from energy companies in Texas, northern Louisiana and southern New Mexico from Sept. 16 through Sept. 24. The survey is closely followed because it provides a snapshot of conditions in one of the most important U.S. oil-producing regions.

Oilfield activity increased during the third quarter, although the pace remained below the second quarter’s level. Dallas Fed senior business economist Kunal Patel said rising costs and difficulties securing equipment, workers and rigs may be restraining further growth.

The findings suggest higher crude prices aren’t automatically translating into a new shale drilling boom. Producers must weigh the potential rewards of increased output against the possibility that geopolitical developments could send prices sharply in either direction.

Executives have raised similar concerns in previous Dallas Fed surveys, but the latest responses underscore how the Iran conflict has intensified uncertainty. Some respondents also questioned whether today’s market could experience the kind of extreme price cycle seen during the previous decade, when crude moved from above $100 a barrel to briefly trading below zero.

For energy investors, that uncertainty could favor producers with strong balance sheets and disciplined spending plans while complicating forecasts for drilling activity, production growth and oilfield-service demand.

title: Oil executives warn Iran war volatility makes planning difficult
